items.prompt: Explain the distinction between private-sector and public-sector ownership.
items.canonical_answer: Private individuals or organisations own/control private-sector activity; government owns/controls public-sector activity.
marking_guidance: Difference (1): private ownership/control. Contrast (1): government ownership/control.
objective_titles: Explain the differences between the private and public sector

items.prompt: Explain the ownership-sector classification of an invented factory that is owned and controlled by government, even though it sells manufactured goods.
items.canonical_answer: It is public-sector because government owns and controls it. Manufacturing describes its secondary productive activity rather than its ownership.
marking_guidance: Context (1): government ownership/control. Reason/conclusion (1): establishes public-sector classification independently of manufacturing.
objective_titles: Explain the differences between the private and public sector

items.prompt: Explain the confusion in classifying a government-owned manufacturer as private-sector simply because it belongs to the secondary sector.
items.canonical_answer: Public/private concerns ownership; primary/secondary/tertiary concerns productive activity. Government ownership makes it public-sector while manufacturing makes it secondary-sector.
marking_guidance: Confusion/boundary (1): ownership and activity are different classifications. Test to distinguish (1): identify owner separately from what the enterprise does.
objective_titles: Explain the differences between the private and public sector

items.prompt: Identify the business form for a single individual trading unincorporated and the form for members owning a business to serve shared interests.
items.canonical_answer: Sole proprietor; co-operative.
marking_guidance: Feature/example (1): sole proprietor. Distinction (1): co-operative.
objective_titles: Describe the different forms of business organisations: sole proprietors, partnerships, private companies, public companies, multi-nationals, co-operatives, close corporations, public corporations

items.prompt: Explain why an invented one-person repair business cannot be called informal solely because it is small. The business is registered and keeps the official records required in this teaching example.
items.canonical_answer: Size does not decide formal status. The supplied registration and recording facts meet the example’s formal criteria even though ownership and operation are small.
marking_guidance: Confusion/boundary (1): small size is not the formal/informal criterion. Test to distinguish (1): use the supplied registration/recording facts.
objective_titles: Describe the different forms of business organisations: sole proprietors, partnerships, private companies, public companies, multi-nationals, co-operatives, close corporations, public corporations

items.prompt: Explain the distinction between a public limited company owned by private shareholders and a public corporation owned by government.
items.canonical_answer: The first permits public share ownership but is privately owned in the supplied case; the second has the defining state ownership connection. Public has different meanings in the two labels.
marking_guidance: Confusion/difference (1): public share-offer form is distinct from state ownership. Test to distinguish (1): check actual ownership and form, rather than the word public alone.
objective_titles: Describe the different forms of business organisations: sole proprietors, partnerships, private companies, public companies, multi-nationals, co-operatives, close corporations, public corporations

items.prompt: Define sole proprietor.
items.canonical_answer: An individual who owns and operates an unincorporated business.
marking_guidance: Meaning/definition and essential element (1): An individual who owns and operates an unincorporated business.
items.reviewed_unchanged: Re-read after the cited claim revision: the existing specific example or institutional boundary remains correct and needs no learner-text change.

items.prompt: Identify two features of a sole proprietor rather than an incorporated company.
items.canonical_answer: One individual owns the business; it trades without a separate incorporated legal identity. A sole proprietor’s personal exposure to business obligations is commonly called unlimited liability.
marking_guidance: Characteristic (1): individual ownership. Distinction (1): unincorporated identity.

items.prompt: Define partnership.
items.canonical_answer: A business owned by people who agree to operate it together and share its results.
marking_guidance: Meaning/definition and essential element (1): A business owned by people who agree to operate it together and share its results.

items.prompt: Identify two potential resources that partners can combine to support an enterprise.
items.canonical_answer: Finance contributions and complementary skills.
marking_guidance: Feature/example (1): combined finance. Distinct example (1): complementary skills.

items.prompt: Define private company.
items.canonical_answer: An incorporated business whose shares are not offered freely to the general public.
marking_guidance: Meaning/definition and essential element (1): An incorporated business whose shares are not offered freely to the general public.

items.prompt: Identify two features distinguishing a private company from a sole proprietor.
items.canonical_answer: Separate incorporated identity; ownership through shares rather than one unincorporated individual.
marking_guidance: Characteristic (1): separate incorporated identity. Distinction (1): share ownership rather than unincorporated individual ownership.

items.prompt: Define public limited company.
items.canonical_answer: An incorporated company that can offer shares to the public; public in its name does not establish government ownership.
marking_guidance: Meaning/definition and essential element (1): An incorporated company that can offer shares to the public; public in its name does not establish government ownership.

items.prompt: Identify two features of a public limited company without assuming that it is state-owned.
items.canonical_answer: Separate incorporated identity; ability to offer shares to the public.
marking_guidance: Characteristic (1): incorporated identity. Distinction/example (1): access to public share offers.

items.prompt: Define multinational business.
items.canonical_answer: A business controlling production or operations in more than one country.
marking_guidance: Meaning/definition and essential element (1): A business controlling production or operations in more than one country.

items.prompt: Identify the two facts that establish multinational operations in an invented business controlling a workshop in Country A and a distribution operation in Country B.
items.canonical_answer: Control of the workshop in Country A; control of the distribution operation in Country B.
marking_guidance: Feature (1): controlled operation in A. Distinction/example (1): controlled operation in another country, B.

items.prompt: Define co-operative.
items.canonical_answer: A business owned and controlled by members to serve their shared interests.
marking_guidance: Meaning/definition and essential element (1): A business owned and controlled by members to serve their shared interests.

items.prompt: Identify two features establishing a members’ seed-purchasing business as a co-operative.
items.canonical_answer: Members own/control it; its purchasing service serves their shared interests.
marking_guidance: Characteristic (1): member ownership/control. Distinction/example (1): shared member purchasing purpose.

items.prompt: Define close corporation.
items.canonical_answer: An incorporated business owned by members, with a legal identity separate from them.
marking_guidance: Meaning/definition and essential element (1): An incorporated business owned by members, with a legal identity separate from them.

items.prompt: Identify two features of a close corporation without asserting a statutory membership limit.
items.canonical_answer: Member ownership; separate incorporated identity.
marking_guidance: Characteristic (1): member ownership. Distinction (1): separate incorporated identity.

items.prompt: Define public corporation.
items.canonical_answer: An enterprise established or owned by the state to undertake economic activity.
marking_guidance: Meaning/definition and essential element (1): An enterprise established or owned by the state to undertake economic activity.

items.prompt: Identify two supplied facts that establish the public-corporation form: an invented water enterprise is owned by the state and undertakes water supply.
items.canonical_answer: State ownership; undertaking economic water-supply activity.
marking_guidance: Characteristic (1): state ownership. Distinction/example (1): economic water-supply activity.

items.prompt: Evaluate converting the business from a sole proprietor to a private company. Invented Namibian business: Copper Acacia Repairs has N$30,000 available but needs N$120,000 for proposed expansion. Its owner values control but may share ownership with an investor. The investor has expressed interest but has not committed funds.
items.canonical_answer: A private company can organise new share ownership and separate the enterprise’s identity, helping accommodate expansion finance. However, the owner may lose some control and faces additional governance responsibilities. The investor’s interest is not guaranteed finance. Choose incorporation if acceptable investment terms and expected expansion benefits justify those costs; otherwise scale back or retain sole ownership while reconsidering finance.
marking_guidance: Argument for (2): permits additional ownership finance (1), helping the stated expansion requirement (1). Argument against (2): shared control (1), additional governance responsibilities (1). Condition (1): acceptable finance terms and credible expansion benefits. Judgement (2): prefer a private company under that condition (1), explicitly recognise investor interest is not a funding commitment (1). Total 7.

items.prompt: Define sole proprietor (2). Identify the ownership sectors of an invented government-owned water enterprise and a privately owned repair shop (2). Explain a difference between a private company and a public limited company concerning shares (2). Identify two constraints relevant to choosing a form for a business needing expansion funds while its owner wants control (2).
items.canonical_answer: A sole proprietor is an individual owning and operating an unincorporated business. The water enterprise is public-sector and the repair shop private-sector. A private company does not offer shares freely to the general public, while a public limited company can offer them to the public. Finance requirements and the owner’s control preference are relevant constraints.
marking_guidance: Meaning (2): individual ownership/operation (1), unincorporated business (1). Separate points for identification (2): public-sector water enterprise (1), private-sector repair shop (1). Share distinction (2): restricted general public access in a private company (1), public offer possible for the public limited company (1). Distinct constraints (2): finance needed (1), control preference (1). Marks allocation 8.

items.prompt: Invented Namibian business: Copper Acacia Repairs has N$30,000 available but needs N$120,000 for proposed expansion. Its owner values control but may share ownership with an investor. The investor has expressed interest but has not committed funds. The enterprise is currently privately owned and unincorporated. Describe three ownership/form features of its current position (6). Explain how admitting an investor through a private company could change finance and control (7). Discuss whether conversion is the most appropriate choice (7).
items.canonical_answer: One individual owns it; it trades without an incorporated identity; it belongs to the private sector. A private company can issue an ownership interest to a suitable investor, potentially adding funds for expansion. New ownership normally brings participation rights, reducing the original owner’s exclusive control; incorporation adds governance responsibilities and a separate identity. Conversion can address the large finance requirement, but the investor has not committed and acceptable terms matter. Support it only if credible finance and expansion benefits outweigh lost control and administration; otherwise a smaller expansion may be preferable.
marking_guidance: Context/data description (6): individual owner (1), not several co-owners (1); unincorporated form (1), no separate incorporated identity (1); private sector (1), ownership is not governmental (1). Mechanism/explanation (7): private share ownership can accommodate investor (1); contribution adds finance (1), supporting equipment/resources (1); ownership rights shared (1), reducing exclusive control (1); company identity separate (1), governance responsibilities added (1). Both sides/judgement (7): funding potential supports expansion (1), separate identity can support continuity (1); control sacrificed (1), administration required (1); investor not committed (1); prefer conversion (1) only if acceptable finance/benefits justify costs (1). Marks allocation 6+7+7=20.

items.prompt: Evaluate the appropriate business form in two seven-mark response plans. Invented Case 1: a Namibian repair owner needs a small improvement affordable from savings, strongly prefers direct control and has manageable commitments. Case 2: the same business proposes major expansion beyond the owner’s resources, suitable investors may contribute ownership finance, and the owner can accept shared control but must assess terms. Compare remaining a sole proprietor with forming a private company.
items.canonical_answer: Case 1: sole ownership preserves control and avoids unnecessary corporate responsibilities, although dependence on one person and personal exposure remain disadvantages. It is suitable if the modest activity and risks remain manageable. Case 2: a private company can accommodate investors and a separate identity, but control is shared and administration grows. Prefer conversion if credible investment on acceptable terms and expansion benefits justify those disadvantages; expressions of interest alone do not settle the choice. A sole proprietor’s personal exposure to business obligations is commonly called unlimited liability.
marking_guidance: Case 1 allocation (7): argument for direct control (1), modest finance already affordable (1); argument against owner dependence (1), unincorporated personal exposure (1); condition manageable scale/commitments (1); judgement retains sole ownership (1) because incorporation adds little under those conditions (1). Case 2 marks (7): argument for additional ownership finance (1), supports expansion beyond personal resources (1); argument against shared control (1), administration (1); condition acceptable committed investment and benefits (1); judgement favours private company (1) conditional on those terms rather than assuming finance (1). Total 14.
